My mother the queen lies dead;

outputs.L2:
My mother, who reigned as queen, has passed away. My father, the king, has grown elderly. He struggles to keep hold of his golden crown and lingers in memories of a time now long gone.

Young men gaze upon my features, yet none can hold my eyes steadily—Cavan, who stands as high as a spear, and Orra, who runs with great speed.

My hand has always come at the cost of death, ever since I first became a woman. Whenever I imagine any man of Gaelic blood, my heart turns cold as if kin to frost.

The one I anticipate is someone different, though I have yet to press my lips against his blade. It is him alone who shall be my master, whether he arrives this evening or in days to come.

Within my chest, a star swells larger. Even now it calls out plainly to the matching star mounted on the gleaming bow of his ship, sailing somewhere distant in the West.

The northern headlands appear faint and shadowy, and the shores facing the wind release a haze where the final great wave broke and delivered the news it carried about him.

I understand that he will bring me grief, warfare, hopelessness, and upheaval—a strange and merciless kind of beauty, along with the spilled crimson blood of kings.

Chest, remain pale for his sake! Lips, stay crimson, ready for his kiss! Spirit, gather strength to hold your joy! Heart, prepare yourself to shatter!

# The Princess's Lament

I am a princess, born to sorrow as much as to sovereignty. My mother, the queen, has passed from this world, and my father, the king, grows old and frail upon his throne. He rules now only in name, his mind wandering the halls of memory, lost among the glories and griefs of days long vanished. The burden of the present falls away from him, and he dwells forever in the past.

The young men of our Gaelic lands look upon me with admiration and desire. They come with hopeful eyes and hearts full of longing, seeking my hand and my affection. Yet I remain cold to them all, indifferent as winter stone. There is a curse upon my love, for since my earliest youth I have brought only death to those who dared to court me. My suitors have fallen, one by one, and so I have learned to feel nothing for the men who surround me.

For I am waiting. Somewhere beyond the horizon, in the lands that lie toward the West, there dwells a lover destined for me alone. I have never seen his face, never heard his voice, and yet I know him to be my only true lord. To him my heart is already given, though he remains a stranger to my eyes.

I sense his approach through signs that others cannot perceive. There is a star burning within my breast, and it calls out across the wide waters to another star—the star that shines upon the prow of his distant galley. Even now he draws nearer, and my soul trembles with the knowledge of his coming.

I know full well what he will bring. He carries with him not only love but sorrow; not only tenderness but battle and bloodshed. Grief will follow in his wake as surely as the tide. And yet I do not turn away. I steel my body, my soul, and my heart to receive him wholly—to embrace both the bliss and the heartbreak that are bound together in his coming. Whatever joy and whatever ruin he brings, I am ready to accept it all.

# The Princess's Vigil

I am the daughter of a dying line. My mother lies beneath the cold stones of our chapel, taken from us in the years when I was still too young to hold her memory as more than fragments—a voice, perhaps, and the warmth of hands that combed my hair. My father, the King, grows ancient now. His beard has gone the white of winter frost, and his hands tremble when they grip the arms of his great chair. The kingdom waits, as I wait, for what must surely come.

They bring me suitors from every glen and holding. The chieftains send their sons, and the sons come dressed in their finest, their brooches gleaming, their swords polished bright. I have watched them ride into our courtyard on their sturdy horses. I have listened to their poets sing my praises and their promises of cattle, land, and lasting peace between our peoples.

I refuse them all.

Let them think me proud. Let them whisper that I am cold, or strange, or touched by some madness born of grief. I care nothing for their judgments. For I know—I have always known—that my heart was never meant for any man who speaks my mother's tongue or knows the hills where I was born.

He comes from the West. This I have seen in dreams and waking visions both. Across the grey and heaving sea, his galley cuts the waves, its sail dark against the horizon, its oars rising and falling like the wings of some great seabird. He is a lord of foreign lands, and I do not know his name, yet I know his face as I know my own reflection in still water.

I do not deceive myself with gentle hopes. This love will not be soft. When he steps upon our shore, he will bring the clash of iron and the cries of dying men. There will be fire in the night and blood upon the sand. Armies will muster, and brothers will fall, and the songs they sing afterward will be laments. He carries doom the way another man might carry gifts—wrapped and certain, meant for me alone.

And still I wait for him.

Let sorrow come. Let battle rage across these ancient lands. I would rather burn in one bright hour of love, though it consume me utterly, than live a hundred quiet years in the arms of men I do not want. This is my fate, and I do not shrink from it. I open my arms to the storm.

Let him come from the West, my destined one, my ruin and my joy. I am ready. I have been ready all my life.

# The Power of Small Words: And, The, But

Some of the most important words in the English language are also among the shortest. Words like "and," "the," and "but" may seem simple, but they play essential roles in how we communicate every day.

## The

"The" is one of the most common words in English. It is called a definite article because it points to something specific. When we say "the book," we mean a particular book, not just any book. Without "the," our sentences would feel incomplete and unclear. This tiny word helps us focus on exactly what we are talking about.

## And

"And" is a connector. It brings words, ideas, and sentences together. Whether we are making a list of items or joining two thoughts, "and" links them smoothly. For example, "I bought apples and oranges" shows how this word unites separate things into one flowing statement. It helps our language feel connected and complete.

## But

"But" introduces contrast. It signals that something different or unexpected is coming. When we say, "I wanted to go outside, but it was raining," the word "but" shows the conflict between our wish and reality. This little word adds depth to our sentences by showing exceptions, differences, and surprises.

## Conclusion

Although "and," "the," and "but" are small, they carry great importance. They help us build clear, connected, and meaningful sentences. These humble words prove that size does not determine value. In fact, our everyday communication would be nearly impossible without them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a warrior princess in ancient Ireland who is waiting for a foreign lover destined to bring her both passion and destruction. Use a formal, lyrical style with short rhyming quatrains.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Watcher on the Cliffs

Upon these cliffs of storm and stone
I stand where salt winds rend the sky,
A princess-warrior, fierce, alone,
And wait for one whose ships draw nigh.

My spear has drunk of many foes,
My name is sung in hall and glen,
Yet still my restless spirit knows
A stranger comes from mortal men.

The druids warned in whispered breath:
"He bears you love, he bears you doom—
Your bridal bed shall be your death,
Your marriage feast shall be your tomb."

Let come the storm, let come the tide,
Let come the sail of foreign make;
I'll take him as both love and bride,
And gladly burn for passion's sake.

For what is life that flows too long,
A quiet fire that never leaps?
I'd rather blaze in fatal song
Than fade where sleeping safety keeps.

So blow, wild wind, and part the mist,
And bring him swift across the foam—
These warrior lips shall yet be kissed
Before the dark that calls me home.

I wait. My hair unbound and free,
My sword still sharp, my heart laid bare;
Come, foreign love, and ruin me—
I've named my fate, and do not care.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue-style poem spoken by a Celtic queen's daughter mourning her dead mother and aging father, longing for a legendary man she has never met who will arrive by galley from the West.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Waiting at Dún Aengus

I stand where the grey stone shoulders the sea,
where my mother's people carved the world in rings,
and I watch the West as she taught me to watch—
though her eyes are closed now, closed with the coins
they pressed cold upon her, closed against the light
she loved, the low gold light of evening.

Mother.

They burned the wrong herbs at your passing.
I would have gathered the right ones, the meadowsweet,
the bog-myrtle you crushed between your queenly fingers
to teach me their names in the old tongue,
the tongue that dies now in my father's throat.

He calls me by your name sometimes.
He sits by the fire and his beard has gone
the color of ash, the color of the sea's underside,
and his hands that held the spear at Mag Tuired
tremble on the arm of the carved chair,
tremble like the last leaves that will not fall.

*Where is your mother?* he asks the smoke.
And I have no lie left kind enough to give him.

So I climb. I climb to the cliff's blind edge
and I look for the one they promised me—
the man from beyond the ninth wave,
whose coming was sung before my breasts had risen,
whose galley the poets swore would breast the swell
some grey dawn, oars flashing like herring-shoals,
his sail the red of the rowan, the red of a wound
that heals into something like a crown.

I have never seen his face.
I have made it a hundred times from the foam,
unmade it a hundred times when the wave collapsed.
I have given him my mother's laughing mouth.
I have given him my father's warrior stillness.
I have given him everything I am losing.

Come now, stranger. Come now, while I am still
the girl the prophecy wanted, before the frost
takes the black from my hair as it took hers.
Come before I become the woman at the fire
asking the smoke where all my people went.

The sea keeps nothing it does not choose to keep.
It kept my mother's ashes. It keeps your keel
somewhere past the drowned edge of the map,
past the place where the sun goes down to die
and is not, they say, entirely dead.

I am the daughter of a dying line.
I am the last watch on the western wall.
And I will stand here in the wind's cold mouth
until you come, or until I too am legend—
a grey shape the fishermen point out to sons:
*There. She waited. There she waits.*

The light is going.
The light my mother loved is going down.

Come by water. Come by the road of whales.
Come while there is still a hand to reach for yours,
still a voice to say the word for *welcome*
in the tongue that will die with me
if you do not, oh you do not,
come.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a mythic, romantic poem about a princess who feels cold toward the men of her own people but is drawn by fate and a star in her breast toward a foreign lord who will bring beauty, battle, and the blood of kings.
counterfactuals.output:
The Star Beneath Her Breast

Cold as the snow on the northern crown
she moved through halls of her father's name,
where suitors knelt and laid their swords down,
and every one of them looked the same—

sons of the fjord, the hearth, the field,
broad in the shoulder, dull in the eye,
each with a shield her hand should wield,
each with a life she would not buy.

They spoke of cattle, of amber, of gold,
of lands that bordered her father's lands,
and she smiled the way that the moon is cold,
and gave them nothing but her hands.

For something burned where her heart should rest—
a small fierce light, an ember, a scar—
a fate sewn quick beneath her breast,
the trembling seed of a foreign star.

It woke her nights. It pulled her gaze
past the safe grey line of her people's shore,
out where the sea-roads split like a maze
toward a name she had never heard before.

*He comes,* it sang, *from a bloodier sun,
a lord of the ships and the burning oar,
and the thread of your life and the thread he spun
were cut to be knotted—and knotted for war.*

She saw him first in the fever of dream:
a dark prow breaking her father's bay,
a banner the color of arterial stream,
and eyes that took the breath away.

Not gentle. No. She did not ask gentle.
She asked for the thing that the star had sworn—
a love like a wound, exalted, elemental,
beauty and battle and kingdoms born.

And when at last the true keels came,
the horns rang red along the strand,
and half her city fell to flame,
and half her kin died sword in hand—

she stood on the wall with the wind in her hair
and felt no grief for the falling town,
for there in the smoke and the salt-bright air
rode the man who would break her father down.

He looked up once. The star replied.
Across the ruin their glances met,
and she knew the way a bride is a bride:
not by the ring, but by the debt.

So let them mourn her, cold and strange,
the men she scorned in her father's hall.
She was never theirs to hold or change—
she was made for the one who would take it all.

The blood of kings ran into the tide.
The gulls came down where the banners fell.
And the princess laughed, and went to his side,
and the star in her breast was quiet at last, and well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical Irish-themed poem with strong imagery of the sea, galleys, northern capes, and a heroine steeling her body and soul for a doomed but longed-for love.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Galley of Ardnamurchan

Grey the sea that beats the northern cape,
Where cormorants scatter from the spray,
And I stand watching for a single shape—
A galley cutting westward through the day.

The salt has cracked my lips to bitter stone,
The wind has combed the wildness from my hair,
Yet still I wait upon this shore alone
For one who promised he would meet me there.

O bind me, body, to this granite ledge,
And let the cold Atlantic teach me steel—
For love that founders on a knife's grey edge
Is sweeter than a hundred safer weals.

I see his oars like herons breaking white,
His sail a wound of crimson in the mist,
And though I know the ending of this night,
I would not trade the promise we have kissed.

They say the man is doomed who crosses there,
Past Mingary, past the drowned men's bell—
That she who loves him weds a widow's care,
And makes her marriage-bed a hollow shell.

Then let me be the widow of the wave,
The keening woman on the northern strand;
I'll take my love though love should dig his grave,
And hold his salt-cold face between my hands.

The heather burns to purple on the brae,
The gulls cry down the corries, wild and thin—
Come, doomed and dear, come cut across the bay;
My soul is armoured. Let the dark begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem titled something like "The Princess" in an early 20th-century Romantic style, using apostrophe to the speaker's own breast, mouth, soul, and heart in the final stanza as she prepares for her destined lover.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Princess

Behind the ivied walls she waits,
Her window turned toward morning's fire,
Where dawn unlocks the eastern gates
And crowns the hills with gold desire.

The years have made her patient, wise;
She weaves the hours on silver thread,
And watches with her seaward eyes
The road her destined love must tread.

No painted lord, no gilded man
Who counts his acres, hoards his crown—
But he whose coming Heaven began
Before the stars were written down.

She hears him in the rising wind,
She feels him in the turning tide;
The dreams her sleeping heart has sinned
Have named him lover, named him guide.

And now the hour draws slowly near
When roads shall meet and fate be sealed;
She feels his footstep, low and clear,
Across the far and folded field.

O breast, be still, and cease to leap!
O mouth, grow sweet with all I am!
O soul, awaken from your sleep
And meet him gentle as a lamb!

O heart, my long-imprisoned bird,
Now sing the song you kept unsung—
For he has come, and at his word
The world, the world is young, is young!
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
